analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in two steps, with carve-outs for small businesses, tipped workers, and teen trainees.
analysis.headline: The federal minimum wage rose from $3.35 to $4.25 over two years after the House passed it 382-37, the Senate 89-8, and the President signed it into law in November 1989.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill raises the federal minimum wage from $3.35 an hour — a level frozen since 1981 — to $3.80 in 1990 and $4.25 in 1991. To win business support, it also raises the "tip credit" so employers can count half the minimum wage as tips, allows a below-minimum training wage for workers under 20 for up to 180 days, and exempts small firms with under $500,000 in annual sales from coverage. It applies wage, overtime, and child labor protections to House of Representatives and Architect of the Capitol employees, who previously were not covered by the law Congress wrote for everyone else.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage hourly workers get the biggest gain: a 27% raise over two years on a wage floor that had not moved in eight years. Workers in Puerto Rico get a scheduled path to the full federal minimum. House and Capitol architect employees gain the same wage, overtime, and child labor protections as private-sector workers. Employers benefit from offsets: a larger tip credit, a subminimum training wage for teens, and a higher small-business exemption.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minimum wage and other low-wage workers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $3.35 to $3.80 on April 1, 1990 and to $4.25 on April 1, 1991 — the first increase since 1981, worth a 27% raise for workers at the bottom.

Extends the Fair Labor Standards Act's wage, overtime, and child labor protections to employees of the House of Representatives and the Architect of the Capitol, closing a gap in which Congress's own workplaces were exempt from the law's protections.
Adds civil money penalties for repeated or willful violations, giving the Labor Department a stronger tool against employers who break wage and hour rules.

Sets a scheduled path for Puerto Rico's lowest-paid industries to reach the full federal minimum wage, with the slowest group (some government workers in industries averaging under $4.00 an hour) reaching it by April 1996.
Exempts up to ten hours a week of time spent in remedial education from overtime rules, so workers can take literacy or basic-education classes without costing their employer overtime pay.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage labor — restaurants, retail, and small businesses — bear the higher payroll. The bill cushions them: businesses with under $500,000 in annual sales are exempted from coverage (existing covered small firms stay at $3.35 without the raises), the tip credit rises from 40% to 50% of the minimum so tipped-employee cash costs rise less, and teens under 20 can be paid the old $3.35 training wage for up to 180 days. Tipped workers and young workers bear part of the cost themselves through those carve-outs.

drawbacks.text: The tip credit rises from 40% to 50% of the minimum wage, letting employers count half of a tipped worker's pay as tips. That lowers the guaranteed cash wage employers must pay, so part of the raise to tipped workers is paid by their customers' tips instead of their employer.

The new training wage lets employers pay workers under 20 the old $3.35 rate — below the new minimum — for 90 days, extendable to 180 days with Labor Department certification, and it expires in March 1993. It creates a legal subminimum aimed at young workers during the period the adult minimum is rising.

The small-business exemption threshold rises from $362,500 to $500,000 in annual sales, removing some firms from coverage entirely; firms newly exempt as of March 31, 1990 stay frozen at $3.35 an hour and never get the increase.

The version as introduced created a Minimum Wage Review Board to review economic data annually and recommend future adjustments; the final law dropped that mechanism, so there is no automatic protection against the new $4.25 eroding until Congress acts again.

For Puerto Rico's lowest-wage industries, full federal minimum coverage is phased in over up to six years, to April 1996 for some categories, so many Puerto Rican workers wait far longer than stateside workers for the same wage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: a 27% increase in the wage floor for millions of workers whose wage had been frozen since 1981, plus stronger penalties for violators and coverage for previously exempt congressional workplaces. The cost is real too, but the bill was deliberately engineered to soften it for business — through the tip credit, the teen training wage, and the higher small-business exemption — and those offsets come at the expense of the very workers near the bottom (tipped workers, teenagers, and workers at newly exempt small firms). The dropped annual-review mechanism means the gain erodes over time unless Congress returns to it. On balance, a substantial and genuine win for low-wage workers, trimmed at the edges by concessions.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 382-37 and the Senate 89-8, senators rejected amendments to weaken it, and President George H.W. Bush signed it into law as Public Law 101-157.

narrative.text: Introduced in June 1989 and referred to the Education and Labor Committee, the bill was amended in subcommittee and full committee markup, reported amended on September 26, 1989, and received an unfavorable comment from the Department of Labor during markup.
The House considered it under a rule barring amendments and passed it 382-37 on November 1, 1989.
The Senate rejected weakening amendments offered by Senators Symms and Gramm, tabling them 64-34 and 63-35, with Democrats voting nearly unanimously to table and most Republicans on the other side.
The Senate then passed the bill without amendment 89-8 on November 8, 1989 — all 53 voting Democrats and 36 of 45 Republicans in favor.
President George H.W. Bush signed it on November 17, 1989, making it Public Law 101-157.
The final law kept the two-step increase but dropped the introduced bill's Minimum Wage Review Board and its annual process for recommending future wage adjustments.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Minimum wage workers gained a 27% raise, and employers of low-wage labor also came out ahead relative to what Congress first proposed, winning the tip credit increase, the teen training wage, and the higher small-business exemption as the price of their support.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage workers, plus employers who won carve-outs

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was overwhelmingly bipartisan — 382-37 in the House and 89-8 in the Senate, with every voting Democrat and 36 of 45 Republicans in favor — and the only sharp party splits came on the Republican-drafted weakening amendments, which Democrats voted to table 50-3 and 48-5 while most Republicans voted the other way.

industries.note: The bill raises what restaurants must pay their lowest-wage staff, but the tip credit rising to 50% lets them count half the minimum wage as tips, cutting the required cash wage for tipped employees — and restaurant tips come out of customers' pockets. The industry gained a large offset as the price of accepting the increase.

industries.industry: Small businesses with under $500,000 in annual sales
industries.note: The bill raises the coverage exemption threshold from $362,500 to $500,000, taking these firms outside the wage and overtime law; firms newly exempt are frozen at $3.35 an hour, so their workers never see the raise.

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: These employers face a 27% higher wage floor over two years, softened only by the teen training wage and remedial-education overtime carve-out. Their interest in blocking or diluting the increase ran against the workers it would pay.

The bill directs regulations treating computer systems analysts and similarly skilled workers as overtime-exempt even if paid hourly, as long as they earn at least 6.5 times the minimum — sparing employers overtime costs for a well-paid professional group.
